headline: Plant garlic now — early November is the last good window before the ground freezes hard.

tasks.title: Get garlic in the ground
tasks.detail: This is prime (and nearly last-call) timing for zone 6a. Push cloves 2-3 inches deep, pointy end up, about 6 inches apart, then cover the bed with 4-6 inches of straw or shredded leaves to insulate roots over winter.

tasks.title: Pull the last cold-hardy crops
tasks.detail: Kale, Brussels sprouts, leeks and carrots actually get sweeter after frost, so keep picking. Dig carrots and any root crops before the ground freezes solid, which can come on fast now.

tasks.title: Winterize hoses and spigots
tasks.detail: Drain and disconnect hoses and shut off outdoor faucets before the first hard freeze to avoid burst pipes. Give evergreens and anything newly planted one last deep soak while the soil is still open.

tasks.title: Put spent beds to bed
tasks.detail: Clear out finished annuals and any diseased or pest-ridden debris (trash it, don't compost it), then mulch the bare soil. Leave a few seed heads and sturdy stems standing for birds and overwintering pollinators.

tasks.title: Tuck in spring bulbs
tasks.detail: There's still a window to plant tulips, daffodils and crocus for next spring. Get them in over the next week or two, before the ground locks up for winter.

tasks.title: Hold off on hard pruning
tasks.detail: Resist cutting back most shrubs and perennials until late winter — now it can spur tender growth that won't survive. Once a hard freeze settles in, add a protective mulch layer over perennials and strawberries.
